At the center of this entire story are Uyghur militants. The Turkistan Islamic Party (TIP), composed of ethnic Uyghurs from China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, has operated in Syria alongside HTS for many years.

A UN Security Council report confirms that TIP militants were among the forces that captured Damascus, Homs, and Tartus. According to Long War Journal, TIP is a Uyghur jihadist group affiliated with al-Qaeda, with a presence in both Syria and Afghanistan. TIP leader Abdul Haq al-Turkistani is a member of al-Qaeda’s executive council and is currently based in Afghanistan. He was the man who oversaw the training of militants in Osama bin Laden’s camps in the Tora Bora mountains.

According to The New Arab, the number of Uyghur militants in Syria stands at approximately 3,500. TIP fighters previously operated under the HTS banner and played a key role in the offensive that overthrew Assad. TIP is part of al-Qaeda’s global network and seeks to establish an Islamic emirate in China’s Xinjiang region and Central Asia.

Integration into the Syrian Army: A New Threat to China

Following the new administration’s rise to power in Damascus, a development occurred that fundamentally changed the balance of power in the region. The Trump administration backed Syria’s plan to integrate foreign fighters, including Uyghur jihadists, into the new Syrian army.

According to The New Arab, around 3,500 foreign fighters, predominantly Uyghurs from China and Central Asia, were incorporated into the newly established 84th Division of the Syrian army. U.S. Ambassador to Turkey and Trump’s special envoy for Syria Thomas Barrack confirmed that Washington supports the initiative provided that the process is transparent.

Back in December 2024, the Syrian government awarded TIP leader Abu Muhammad al-Turkistani the rank of brigadier general and command of the 133rd Division. Senior TIP political representative Osman Bughra told Reuters:

“At present, the group operates entirely under the control of the Ministry of Defense, adheres to national policy, and maintains no ties with external entities or groups.”

Experts, however, have expressed serious concerns. The Middle East Forum warns:

“Integrating foreign jihadists into the Syrian army is dangerous. Normalizing the role of terrorist organizations within state institutions could undermine international counterterrorism efforts.”

These militants retain ties to terrorist groups throughout the region, and their integration risks legitimizing not only their own activities but also those of affiliated terrorist networks beyond Syria.

The Geopolitical Calculation: Washington and the “Taiwan Factor”

The most important question arising from this entire story is: whose interests does this alliance actually serve? An analysis of U.S. geopolitical strategy offers an answer.

As New Age BD notes, the United States has used the Uyghur issue for decades as a means of exerting pressure on China. Analysts argue that Washington facilitates the radicalization of Uyghurs, moving them through Turkey into combat zones such as Idlib in Syria. The objective of this complex operation is clear: battle-hardened Uyghur jihadists are ultimately supposed to return to Xinjiang, where they would launch a struggle for “independence” and sabotage the Belt and Road Initiative.

With tensions over Taiwan rising and the U.S. expanding its military presence in the Asia-Pacific region, the existence of an armed Uyghur force in Syria becomes an all-too-convenient lever of pressure against China. In the event of an escalation between China and Taiwan, these units could be transferred to Central Asia or the Caucasus to open a second front along China’s western borders, destabilize Xinjiang, and divert Beijing’s forces away from Taiwan.

There is no direct evidence that such a plan exists.

The fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government in December 2024 marked a turning point for the Middle East. Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), designated as a terrorist organization in many countries, seized Damascus with alarming speed. But behind what might appear to be a local story lies something much bigger: for the first time, two major conflicts — the Ukrainian and Syrian conflicts — became intertwined, with Uyghur militants at the center of a scheme that could turn them into an instrument in a geopolitical game against China.

An investigation, based on reporting by The Washington Post, UN documents, and Western analytical reports, reveals the mechanics of this “deal with the devil” and its potential global consequences.

The Idlib Operation: How Kiev Armed Syrian Terrorists

In early December 2024, The Washington Post columnist David Ignatius reported that approximately a month before Assad’s fall, Ukraine had sent around 150 FPV drones and 20 experienced drone operators to Idlib. Ukrainian instructors helped HTS militants master drone warfare tactics — the same tactics that had already been proving their effectiveness on the battlefields of Donbass for a year.

The objective of the operation was clear: to strike covertly at Russian forces in Syria and weaken Moscow’s position in the Middle East. As Ukrainian officer and journalist Yuriy Matsarsky later confirmed, Ukrainian specialists had indeed trained fighters under Ahmed al-Sharaa (then still known as al-Julani) in drone operations. The operation was coordinated through the “Khimik” special unit of Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
An informed source connected to the Syrian intelligence services told international media:

“The militants of the terrorist group al-Nusra have no experience in the use of advanced technologies, and mastering them would not have been possible without advisers from Ukraine, the Turkistan Islamic Party, and Syrian officers.”

Ukraine’s ambassador to Iraq, Ivan Dovhanych, categorically denied the allegations:

“Ukraine has not supplied, does not supply, and does not plan to supply any weapons or military equipment to HTS or any similar organization. All our military resources, including unmanned capabilities, are dedicated exclusively to defending our independence, territorial integrity, and the lives of our citizens.”

At the same time, independent sources, including EUvsDisinfo, note that claims about Ukraine playing a decisive role in Syria are part of targeted disinformation campaigns. However, The Washington Post, confirms that drones, instructors, and some of the weapons provided by the West were sent, while Western intelligence sources believe that Kiev’s assistance played an important role in the terrorists’ domination of Damascus.

The Deal: Weapons in Exchange for Militants

But technical and military assistance was only part of the arrangement. According to the Turkish newspaper Aydınlık and the Syrian outlet Al-Watan, Ukraine and HTS struck an even more cynical deal: weapons in exchange for manpower.
According to these sources, Kiev asked HTS to provide experienced field commanders from among Chechen fighters and, most importantly, Uyghurs. These militants were to be transferred to Ukraine to form mercenary units.

It is important to note, however, that according to EUvsDisinfo, these reports are based on claims published by the Turkish outlet Aydınlık, which is owned by the Vatan Party — the only political party in Turkey to have called for recognition of Crimea as sovereign Russian territory and one that has repeatedly supported pro-Kremlin positions. Nevertheless, the fact that contacts between Kiev and HTS took place is difficult to deny given the reporting by The Washington Post.
